fields.meta_description: Build a registration form that takes the fee, stops at your cap, starts a waitlist and saves each registrant to a database you own.
fields.h1: Build a Registration Form That Manages Every Registrant
fields.hero_description: Describe who is signing up and for what. Emergent builds the registration form, takes any fee through Stripe and keeps each registrant as a row in your own database.
fields.features_heading: What a Registration Form Has to Handle
fields.features_subheading: Collecting a name is the easy part. These six pieces decide whether the list is still right on the day.
fields.feature_1:
Questions that change with each answer

Show a meal question only to dinner guests, or a company field only to business buyers. Emergent writes that logic from your description and keeps hidden answers out of the record.
fields.feature_2:
Caps and a waitlist on any option

Set a limit per ticket type or session. When one fills, the form stops offering it and adds new registrants to a waitlist, then offers a freed spot to the next name in line.
fields.feature_3:
Fees taken before a spot is confirmed

Connect Stripe and take the registration fee as part of submitting. The row stays pending until the payment clears, and a refund or cancellation hands the spot back to the list.
fields.feature_4:
Uploads checked before approval

Ask for a permit or a receipt and hold the registration until someone reviews it. Emergent can read dates and numbers off an upload and flag a file that is missing or out of date.
fields.feature_5:
Confirmations and reminders by email

Send each registrant a confirmation with their details and a link to change them. Schedule a reminder before the date, and post a daily count of new sign-ups to a Slack channel.
fields.feature_6:
Code you can take with you

Publish on your own domain or embed the form on a site you already run. Export the full code to GitHub when a developer wants registrations inside the product your team maintains.

fields.usecase_heading: Registration Forms for Four Kinds of Lists
fields.tab_content_1:
180 seats sold, then a waitlist takes over

Harbor Food Bank sells 180 seats to its spring dinner at $85 each. Guests pick a meal and pay through Stripe Checkout, and a seat is confirmed only when the payment clears. Once the last seat sells, the form turns into a waitlist. A cancellation offers that seat to the first name on it by email.
fields.tab_content_2:
A warranty date read straight off the receipt

Buyers of the Kestrel grinder register it with the serial number and a photo of the receipt. The form reads the purchase date off the photo, adds two years and saves the warranty end date to the buyer's contact in HubSpot. A receipt it cannot read goes to the support queue for a person to check.
fields.tab_content_3:
Hold food vendors until a permit is on file

Every vendor at the Riverside Saturday market registers for a booth and pays the booth fee. Food vendors also upload a county health permit. A food vendor with no permit, or one that expires before market day, is held with the reason shown. Craft and art vendors go straight to booth assignment.
fields.tab_content_4:
Returning gardeners pick their plots first

Elm Street Garden has 40 plots and 52 registrations this spring. Gardeners who held a plot last year get the first week to register and keep their bed. Newcomers fill the plots that are left in the order they signed up. The 12 who miss out join a waitlist ranked by registration time.

fields.howto_title: How to Create a Registration Form
fields.howto_description: Settle who the list is for and what limits it has before you write a single field.
fields.howto_step_2_title: 02 Set the limits before the fields
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Cut every field nobody will read
fields.howto_step_4_title: 04 Choose where the fee is taken
fields.howto_step_1_des: An event seat and a market booth need different records. Write down what one finished registration looks like as a row: the person, what they registered for, what they paid and any document attached to it.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Note every cap, such as seats per ticket type or booths per size. Then decide what happens when a cap is reached: does the form close or switch to a waitlist? Settle who gets a freed spot before anyone asks.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Go through each question and name the person who will use the answer. A caterer reads meal choices; nobody reads a fax number. Remove fields with no reader, and make optional anything only some registrants need to answer.
fields.howto_step_4_des: If there is a fee, take it in the same flow as the details. Pick the payment processor and a refund rule with a cutoff date. Put that rule on the form itself, where registrants read it before they pay anything.
fields.howto_step_5_des: Paste your notes in plain English: the fields, the caps, the fee and who gets alerted. Emergent builds the form along with the registrant table and the emails around it. Change anything later by asking, such as moving a deadline back a week.
fields.howto_step_6_des: Sign up under a made-up name and pay with a Stripe test card. Then cancel, and watch the spot go to the first name on the waitlist. Fix anything that surprised you before the real link goes out to anyone.
fields.howto_step_7_title: 07 Share the link and watch the count
fields.howto_step_7_des: Publish the form on your own domain, or add it to a page people already visit. Put the link where registrants look anyway, such as a newsletter or a QR code at the venue. A daily count in Slack shows how fast spots are going.

plan.angle: The top 10 is mostly DMV PDFs and template galleries from Jotform, SurveyMonkey, Wufoo and Lumin, all of which stop at the form itself. This page treats a registration form as the front door of a list someone has to manage: a seat cap and waitlist, a fee taken at sign-up, documents checked before approval, and every registrant saved as a row in a database the organizer owns. It answers the template, online, free, HTML and PDF searches plainly and shows four registrations whose rules have little in common.
tab_stories: A food bank's spring dinner sells 180 seats in tables of eight, takes payment at registration, and moves the next sign-up to a waitlist once the last seat is gone.

A coffee grinder maker lets buyers register a product with its serial number and a receipt photo, reads the purchase date from the receipt and sets a two-year warranty end date on the customer's record.
A Saturday makers market registers vendors for booths and holds any food vendor who has not uploaded a health permit before a booth is assigned.
A community garden opens 40 plots, gives returning gardeners first pick, and ranks the 12 newcomers who did not get a plot on a waitlist in the order they registered.
